title: Parvulus
summary: Hugo opens the third volume with a portrait of the Paris street child, the gamin: ragged, homeless, foul-mouthed and yet innocent at heart.
details: The narrative pauses to introduce a type rather than a person. Paris, Hugo says, has a child as the forest has a sparrow: the gamin. He is between seven and thirteen, lives in bands, sleeps in the open, wears a man's cast-off trousers and someone else's hat, swears, haunts wine-shops, knows thieves and sings dirty songs.

For all that, Hugo insists, there is no evil in him. He carries innocence in his heart like a pearl that mud cannot dissolve. Asked what this creature is, the great city would answer: it is my little one.

title: Some of His Particular Characteristics
summary: The gamin's habits: his trades, his coinage of scrap copper, his insect fauna and his quick, cynical wit.
details: The gamin sometimes has a shirt, but only one; sometimes shoes, but without soles; sometimes a lodging, which he loves because his mother is there, but he prefers the street for its liberty. His games are founded on hatred of the bourgeois. He earns coppers by calling cabs, letting down carriage steps and laying planks across flooded gutters, and the children trade in a currency of scrap copper they call loques.

He studies the small creatures of the pavements, prizes above all a fabulous monster called 'the deaf thing', and has as many sayings as Talleyrand, though more honest ones. Hugo gives two samples of his repartee, one aimed at a doctor following a funeral, the other at an indignant husband in a crowd.

title: He Is Agreeable
summary: In the evening the gamin becomes the titi of the theatre gallery; Hugo sketches his irreverent taste and his gift for puncturing anything solemn.
details: With a few sous the gamin gets into a theatre, where he is transformed into the titi, the creature of the topmost gallery, whose applause turns that stinking loft into Paradise. Hugo's formula: give a man the useless and deprive him of the necessary, and you have the gamin.

His literary taste is not classical; he nicknamed the actress Mademoiselle Mars 'Mademoiselle Muche'. He fishes in sewers, laughs at everything, mixes hymns with obscenities, and is, Hugo says, Rabelais in childhood. Nothing frightens or astonishes him; he would greet a sea-monster with a jeer.

title: He May Be of Use
summary: Hugo pairs the gamin with the Parisian lounger as the two extremes of the city, and warns that this thoughtful, watching child will grow up.
details: Paris begins with the lounger, who watches passively, and ends with the gamin, inexhaustible initiative; the whole monarchy is in the one and all anarchy in the other. The pale child of the faubourgs grows supple in suffering and watches social realities more closely than he seems to. Prejudice, abuse, tyranny and injustice should beware of him.

Of what clay is he made? The first mud to hand, Hugo answers; but a god has always passed over the gamin, and the spirit of Paris, which makes men of destiny out of children of chance, turns the jug into an amphora.

title: His Frontiers
summary: A digression on the banlieue, the melancholy half-wild fringe of Paris where bands of escaped children play, which is the whole world to the gamin.
details: The gamin loves the city but also solitude, and Hugo, confessing himself a lifelong prowler about the barriers of Paris, describes the strange amphibious country where fields meet roofs: waste ground, quarries, drum practice, tea-gardens by cemeteries, great walls cutting across sunlit land full of butterflies. He lists the familiar spots, from the Glacière to the Pierre-Plate de Châtillon with its rotting trapdoor over an old quarry.

In these limbos one finds groups of ragged children crowned with cornflowers, runaways from poor families, playing marbles round a hole, who, on seeing a stranger, remember they have a trade and offer to sell a stocking full of cockchafers or a bunch of lilacs. Sometimes thin, sunburnt girls are among them. For these children Paris and its suburbs are the universe; nothing exists two leagues beyond the barriers.

title: A Bit of History
summary: On abandoned children: hundreds were picked up each year in Paris, yet Hugo argues the air of the city keeps its street boys inwardly intact, and he recalls how the old monarchy used such children for its galleys.
details: At the time of the story there was no policeman on every corner and stray children abounded; the police picked up some two hundred and sixty homeless children a year under bridges and in building sites. All a man's crimes, Hugo says, begin in the vagabondage of the child. Yet he claims an exception for Paris: the vagabond child elsewhere is a lost man, but the Paris street boy stays almost intact inside, preserved by something in the air of the city like salt in the sea.

This does not lessen the anguish of meeting such a child, trailing the threads of a broken family, 'cast on the pavements of Paris'. The old monarchy did not discourage abandonment, since it hated schooling the people. Under Louis XIV, Colbert needed galley-slaves for the fleet and had street children of fifteen sent to the galleys; under Louis XV children vanished for purposes people only dared whisper about, and when fathers fought the guards who took them, it was the fathers who were hanged.

title: The Gamin Should Have His Place in the Classifications of India
summary: The gamins form almost a caste, with their own standards of prestige: having seen a man fall, having a deep scar, being left-handed, and above all attending executions.
details: The street boys of Paris nearly constitute a caste, which not everyone may join. The word gamin itself, Hugo notes, first reached print in 1834. Respect among them goes to the boy who has seen a man fall from Notre-Dame, who has stolen lead from statues, or who 'knows' a soldier; the great lament is never yet to have seen anyone fall from a fifth-floor window.

Irreverence in religion is a point of honour: a condemned man listening to his confessor in the cart is mocked for 'talking to his black cap'. Attending executions is a duty; the boys climb walls, lamps and chimneys to see, give the guillotine pet names, hoot at or admire the victims, and keep a tradition of what every famous criminal wore. A memorable accident, a bad cut 'to the bone', a strong fist, a squint or left-handedness all raise a boy's standing.

title: In Which the Reader Will Find a Charming Saying of the Last King
summary: The gamin swims naked in the Seine, draws pears on walls (once helped by King Louis Philippe himself), hates priests, and knows every policeman in Paris by sight.
details: In summer the gamin turns frog, diving into the Seine from coal barges and laundry boats in defiance of modesty and the police, and warning his fellows with a famous cry when the police arrive. He can always daub, if not read; from 1830 he scrawled pears on walls, and Hugo tells how Louis Philippe, meeting a tiny boy struggling to draw a giant pear on a gate pillar at Neuilly, finished the pear for him and gave him a louis.

He loves uproar and detests priests, though he will serve mass if asked. His two unattainable desires are to overthrow the government and to get his trousers mended. He knows every policeman in Paris by face and habit, with a private verdict on each.

title: The Old Soul of Gaul
summary: Gaminerie is a shade of the Gallic spirit, found in Molière, Beaumarchais and Voltaire; the gamin can pass in a moment from scapegrace to hero, like the drummer-boy Barra.
details: Hugo traces the gamin's spirit through French genius: Poquelin (Molière), the son of the fish-market, Beaumarchais, Voltaire, Camille Desmoulins, the general Championnet who as a boy played irreverent pranks in the churches of Paris. Mixed with good sense, gaminerie strengthens it as alcohol strengthens wine.

The gamin has bad teeth because he is ill-fed and fine eyes because he has wit. He plays in the gutter and stands up in a revolt; his effrontery persists under grapeshot; Barra the drummer-boy was a gamin of Paris. This child of the puddle is also the child of the ideal. In one word: he amuses himself because he is unhappy.

title: Ecce Paris, Ecce Homo
summary: The gamin is at once a grace and a disease of the nation, to be cured by light and education; and since the gamin expresses Paris, Hugo celebrates Paris as the total of all history, Athens, Rome and Jerusalem in one.
details: The gamin is the infant populace with the wrinkle of the old world on his brow, a disease to be cured by light: by science, letters, art and education. Sooner or later France must choose between the children of France and the gamins of Paris.

Then Hugo turns to the city itself. Paris is the ceiling of the human race; everything that exists elsewhere exists there. In a long cascade of parallels he matches Parisian types, places and characters with those of ancient Athens and Rome, from fishwives and tightrope dancers to parasites and dandies, from Père-Lachaise to the Esquiline.

Paris accepts everything, laughs at everything, condones everything provided it is amused; it is all civilisations and all barbarisms in abridgement. And, Hugo adds grimly, it would regret not having a guillotine: a little of the Place de Grève seasons the eternal festival.

title: To Scoff, to Reign
summary: Paris sets the fashion and the law for the world, mixing sublime and burlesque; its light has kindled revolutions and liberators everywhere, and its secret is daring.
details: There is no limit to Paris. It may be stupid when it chooses, and the universe is stupid with it; then it wakes and laughs in the face of the human race. Its gaiety is thunder and its farce holds a sceptre. Its 14th of July delivered the globe, its night of the 4th of August dissolved feudalism, and its light fills Washington, Bolívar, Garibaldi, John Brown and the patriots of a dozen nations; its books and thinkers are the manuals of mankind. Yet the same genius scrawls caricatures on the temple of Theseus and graffiti on the Pyramids.

Paris is a moral being, immense because it dares. To dare is the price of progress: Montesquieu may foresee, Diderot preach and Rousseau premeditate the Revolution, but Danton had to dare it. The cry 'Audacity!' is a fiat lux, and the same lightning runs from the torch of Prometheus to Cambronne's short pipe.

title: The Future Latent in the People
summary: The Parisian populace is a grown-up gamin; Hugo appeals to philosophers to bring light to the barefoot masses of the faubourgs, whose rags may be turned to crystal.
details: To paint the child is to paint the city: the Parisian people, even grown, remains the street arab. The true Parisian race lives in the faubourgs, where it toils and suffers, among unknown beings from the porter of La Râpée to the knacker of Montfaucon. Cicero called them the dregs of the city and Burke the mob.

What does it matter that they go barefoot and cannot read? Hugo asks. Should they be abandoned for that? He calls on philosophers to teach, enlighten and sow enthusiasm, to spend their alphabets lavishly and proclaim rights. This crowd may be made sublime; the sand trodden underfoot, cast in the furnace, becomes the crystal through which Galileo and Newton discover stars.

title: Little Gavroche
summary: Eight or nine years after the events of Volume II, a merry, unloved eleven-year-old street boy called Little Gavroche roams the Boulevard du Temple; his family, the destitute Jondrettes, live in the Gorbeau hovel next to a poor young man known as M. Marius.
details: Eight or nine years after the second part of the story, a boy of eleven or twelve could be seen about the Boulevard du Temple and the Château-d'Eau who matched Hugo's ideal gamin in every point but one: behind the laugh of his age his heart was sombre and empty. He wore a man's trousers and a woman's chemise, given in charity, not by his parents. He had a father and mother, yet was an orphan, for his father did not think of him and his mother did not love him. The street was kinder to him than his mother's heart, and he was merry because he was free.

Every two or three months he said, 'I'll go and see mamma,' and walked down to the Salpêtrière quarter, to the house numbered 50–52 the reader already knows: the Gorbeau hovel. It was now, unusually, full of lodgers, all poor. The old principal tenant of Jean Valjean's day had died and been replaced by another, Madame Bourgon, remarkable only for her succession of three parakeets.

The most wretched household there was a family of four, father, mother and two grown daughters, in one attic room. The father had given his name as Jondrette, and had told the portress that anyone asking for a Pole, an Italian or a Spaniard meant him. This was the boy's family. When he came, he found a cold hearth and cold hearts, and was asked where he came from and where he was going; his answer was 'the street'. His mother loved his sisters, not him.

On the boulevard the boy was called Little Gavroche, probably, Hugo says, because his father's name was Jondrette: wretched families like to break the thread. The Jondrettes' room was the last along the corridor; the cell next to it was occupied by a very poor young man called M. Marius. Hugo promises to explain who this M. Marius was.

title: Ninety Years and Thirty-Two Teeth
summary: Portrait of M. Gillenormand in 1831: a hale, loud, cane-wielding bourgeois of over ninety, a relic of the eighteenth century, with a spinster daughter past fifty whom he scolds like a child.
details: In the streets near the Temple a few old inhabitants still remember M. Gillenormand, who was very much alive in 1831. He was over ninety, walked erect, talked loudly, ate, drank and snored, had all thirty-two of his teeth and wore spectacles only to read. The complete and rather haughty bourgeois of the eighteenth century, he claimed to have renounced women ten years before, not because he was too old but, he said, because he was too poor: he had about fifteen thousand francs a year and dreamed of an inheritance to spend on mistresses.

He was quick-tempered and beat people with his cane when contradicted, as men did in the great century. He had an unmarried daughter over fifty whom he scolded savagely and would gladly have whipped; to him she seemed eight years old. He boxed his servants' ears and was shaved daily by a barber who hated him out of jealousy over a pretty barberess. He prided himself on his penetration and loved the words 'the sensible man' and 'nature', by which he meant that civilisation gnaws and claws where savages devour.

title: Like Master, Like House
summary: M. Gillenormand's house in the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, his tapestries, his boudoir and his Directory dress; he has had two wives and holds the French Revolution to be a heap of blackguards.
details: He owned and lived in No. 6 Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire in the Marais, in a vast first-floor apartment between street and garden hung with Gobelins and Beauvais pastorals, his bed enclosed in a nine-leaved Coromandel screen. A short staircase from his window led into the garden, which he climbed nimbly. He treasured a boudoir hung with flowered straw made by Louis XIV's convicts, inherited from a centenarian great-aunt.

He had had two wives. His manners lay between those of a courtier he had never been and a lawyer he might have been; he had been the kind of husband always deceived by his wives and never by his mistresses. He was a connoisseur of painting and owned a portrait by Jordaens of no one knows whom. He dressed like an Incroyable of the Directory, in swallowtail coat, knee-breeches and buckled shoes, and pronounced that the French Revolution was a heap of blackguards.

title: Luc-Esprit
summary: Gillenormand's youthful memories of dancers at the opera, his contempt for modern politicians, and his coarse frankness; his godfather named him Luc-Esprit.
details: At sixteen, ogled at the opera by two famous beauties at once, he had retreated towards an obscure little dancer his own age named Nahenry. He abounded in such memories, rhapsodised about the dancer Guimard's finery and a waistcoat of his youth, and had been called 'a charming fool' by Madame de Boufflers.

He read the newspapers only to laugh at the vulgar names of the men in power, imagining the farce of 'M. Gillenormand, minister'. He called everything by its name, decent or not, even before ladies, with an elegant lack of embarrassment that belonged to his century. His godfather had predicted genius for him and given him the names Luc-Esprit.

title: A Centenarian Aspirant
summary: Gillenormand's lifelong pride in a school prize given by the Duc de Nivernais, his faith in the 'elixir of gold', his adoration of the Bourbons and horror of 1789, and his hope of living to a hundred.
details: Born at Moulins, he had won school prizes there and been crowned by the Duc de Nivernais, whom he called the Duc de Nevers and considered the great figure of the century; neither the Convention nor Napoleon had effaced the memory. He believed Catherine the Great had atoned for partitioning Poland by buying the secret of the 'elixir of gold', a cure for the catastrophes of love, and would have been furious to learn it was merely perchloride of iron.

He adored the Bourbons and had a horror of 1789, forever recounting how his gaiety and cleverness had saved his head during the Terror. Praise of the Republic in his presence made him purple with rage. Alluding to his ninety years he would say he hoped not to see ninety-three twice, hinting that he meant to live to a hundred.

title: Basque and Nicolette
summary: Gillenormand's theory that a philandering husband should let his wife ruin him, which his second wife duly did; his two servants, whom he renames Basque and Nicolette.
details: He held that a man fond of women and saddled with a disagreeable wife should hand her the purse-strings: she would busy herself with leases, lawsuits and notaries, feel herself sovereign, and console herself for his disdain by ruining him. He had applied the theory; his second wife had so managed his fortune that, when widowed, he had just enough to sink into an annuity of fifteen thousand francs, most of which would die with him. He did not mind, having no wish to leave property behind and no faith in the public debt.

He kept two servants, a man and a woman, and rebaptised each one who entered his service. Men got the name of their province; his last valet, a stout, short-winded fellow of fifty-five from Bayonne, became 'Basque'. Every maid was called Nicolette, including a certain Magnon of whom, Hugo says, more will be heard. When a haughty cook named Olympie asked thirty francs a month, he offered fifty on condition she be called Nicolette.

title: In Which Magnon and Her Two Children Are Seen
summary: A dismissed maid, Magnon, twice sends Gillenormand a newborn boy and names him as father; flattered, he denies paternity but agrees to pay for both children. His late priest brother, his two daughters, and the despised son-in-law who was a colonel at Waterloo.
details: Gillenormand turned sorrow into wrath and prided himself on remaining a gallant, which he called 'royal renown'. When he was eighty-four, a maid dismissed six months earlier sent him a yelling newborn boy in a basket and attributed it to him. Amid the household's uproar he was not angry at all; flattered, he cited aged fathers from history, declared the child none of his, and ordered it cared for. The woman, Magnon, sent a second boy the following year. He capitulated, returned both to their mother with eighty francs a month for their keep, on condition she stop, and insisted on visiting them from time to time, which he did.

He had had a brother, a priest and rector of the Academy of Poitiers for thirty-three years, a peaceable miser who gave alms only in bad or demonetised sous. Gillenormand himself gave gladly and nobly and liked everything about him done grandly, even his own fleecing; cheated in an inheritance, he complained only that he had been badly robbed.

By his first wife he had a daughter who remained unmarried; by his second, a daughter who died at about thirty, having married for love a soldier of fortune who had served the Republic and the Empire, won the cross at Austerlitz and been made colonel at Waterloo. 'He is the disgrace of my family,' said the old bourgeois. He took much snuff and believed very little in God.

title: Rule: Receive No One Except in the Evening
summary: Gillenormand, frivolous and great, lived in the Faubourg Saint-Germain during the early Restoration and retired to the Marais after eighty, keeping his door shut all day and receiving only after dinner at five.
details: Such was Luc-Esprit Gillenormand, grey-haired rather than white, venerable in spite of everything, with something of the eighteenth century about him: frivolous and great.

In 1814 and the early Restoration, when he was a mere seventy-four, he lived in the Rue Servandoni near Saint-Sulpice, and only withdrew to the Marais when he quit society after eighty. There he walled himself in his habits. The chief was to keep his door closed all day and receive no one, not even the king, before evening: he dined at five, and after that his door was open. The day, he said, is vulgar and deserves a closed shutter.

title: Two Do Not Make a Pair
summary: Gillenormand's two daughters: the younger, who married the man of her dreams and died; the elder, Mademoiselle Gillenormand, a prude and bigot who keeps house for her father and dotes on a lancer grand-nephew, Théodule. In the house there is also a small boy, the old man's grandson, whom he bullies and idolises.
details: The two daughters were born ten years apart and were nothing alike. The younger had a charming soul turned toward flowers, verses and music, wedded in imagination to a vague heroic figure; the elder dreamed of a rich contractor or prefect for a husband and the glories of being 'Madame la Préfète'. One had wings like an angel, the other like a goose. The younger married the man of her dreams, and died. The elder never married.

When she enters the story she is an antique virtue and incombustible prude with a sharp nose and a dull mind; no one outside the family knows her first name, and she is simply 'Mademoiselle Gillenormand the elder'. Her modesty is carried to excess (she cherishes the frightful memory of a man once seeing her garter), yet she allows her grand-nephew Théodule, an officer of Lancers, to kiss her. She is also a bigot, devoted to a rococo chapel, with a chapel friend, Mademoiselle Vaubois, who is even stupider than she is. Age has softened her; she has never been malicious, and there breathes from her the stupor of a life that is finished without ever having begun.

She keeps house for her father, as the Bishop's sister kept house for him. Between the old man and the old maid there is also a child, a little boy, always trembling and mute before M. Gillenormand, who never addresses him except in a severe voice, sometimes with raised cane, calling him rascal and scoundrel. He idolises him. This is his grandson.

title: An Ancient Salon
summary: About 1817 Gillenormand reigns over the ultra-Royalist salon of Madame de T. in the Rue Férou, where Napoleon is mocked and liberals cursed; he brings his daughter and a handsome boy of seven, pitied as 'poor child' because his father is a 'brigand of the Loire', the despised son-in-law.
details: While living in the Rue Servandoni, Gillenormand frequented aristocratic Royalist salons, where, bourgeois though he was, he was an oracle. About 1817 he spent two afternoons a week at the house of the Baronne de T., widow of a former ambassador to Berlin who had died bankrupt leaving ten volumes of memoirs on Mesmer. Her poor, proud salon was purely Royalist: they sipped tea, groaned at the century, the charter and the Bonapartists, sang fishwives' songs calling Napoleon 'Nicolas', made feeble puns on the ministry and sang their own Ça ira against the Bonapartists. In the Fualdès affair they sided with the accused because the victim was a Bonapartist. The salon's other cock was the Comte de Lamothe-Valois, respected despite, or because of, his part in the affair of the necklace.

Gillenormand's standing was first-rate; his great age and his sallies gave him dignity. He said that all kings who were not King of France were provincial kings, and, seeing Talleyrand pass at a Te Deum, 'There goes his Excellency the Evil One.'

He was always accompanied by his tall daughter, over forty and looking fifty, and by a handsome, rosy little boy of seven with trusting eyes, around whom voices murmured, 'How handsome he is! What a pity! Poor child!' He was called 'poor child' because his father was 'a brigand of the Loire'. This brigand of the Loire was Gillenormand's son-in-law, 'the disgrace of his family'.

title: One of the Red Spectres of That Epoch
summary: At Vernon a scarred, poor old soldier grows flowers: he is Georges Pontmercy, hero of the Republic's and Empire's wars, made colonel and baron at Waterloo, now on half-pay and under surveillance. Gillenormand has taken his son Marius from him on pain of disinheritance; the colonel watches the boy secretly at mass and befriends the curé Mabeuf and his churchwarden brother.
details: Around 1817 a passer-by on the bridge at Vernon might have seen, in the smallest of the walled gardens along the Seine, a bowed man of about fifty in a leather cap and wooden shoes, with a great scar down his face and nearly white hair, hoeing among celebrated tulips and dahlias. He lived alone with a servant woman, saw only the poor and his curé, the Abbé Mabeuf, and opened his door smiling to anyone who came to see his flowers. He was the 'brigand of the Loire'.

He was Georges Pontmercy. Hugo recounts his career: a soldier of the Rhine and Italian armies, wounded at Mont-Palissel, with Joubert at the Col de Tende, at Lodi, at Austerlitz where the Emperor gave him the cross, one of three survivors of the cemetery at Eylau, at Friedland, Moscow, the Berezina, Leipzig and the campaign of France, twenty-seven splinters taken from one arm. He followed Napoleon to Elba. At Waterloo, as chief of a squadron of cuirassiers, he captured the standard of the Lunenburg battalion, took a sabre-cut across the face, and was made colonel, baron and officer of the Legion of Honour on the field; an hour later he fell in the ravine of Ohain, from which, as the reader will remember, he was pulled out.

The Restoration put him on half-pay and sent him to live under surveillance at Vernon, refusing to recognise his rank, title or decoration. He signed himself 'Colonel Baron Pontmercy' regardless, wore his rosette in defiance of threatened prosecution, returned unopened letters addressed to 'Commandant Pontmercy', and asked the crown attorney whether he was permitted to wear his scar. Under the Empire he had married Mademoiselle Gillenormand; she died in 1815 leaving a child, and the grandfather claimed the boy, threatening to disinherit him otherwise. The father yielded for the child's sake and transferred his love to flowers; he was forbidden ever to see or speak to his son.

The boy, Marius, knew he had a father and nothing more, and from the whispers of his grandfather's society came to think of him with shame. Every two or three months the colonel slipped into Paris and hid behind a pillar at Saint-Sulpice to watch his son at mass, afraid of the aunt. The churchwarden there noticed the scarred man weeping, recognised him later at Vernon when visiting his brother the curé, and the two came to know the whole story and venerate him. Twice a year Marius wrote his father duty letters dictated by his aunt; the colonel's tender replies went unread into the grandfather's pocket.

title: Requiescant
summary: Madame de T.'s salon is all Marius knows of the world: a mummified society of aged aristocrats, priests, cardinals and peers, 'ultra' in politics. Hugo explains the ultra spirit of 1814–1820 and the doctrinarians who followed. Marius grows up grave, a fanatical Royalist who dislikes his grandfather and is gloomy about his father.
details: The salon was Marius's one window on life, and it made the once joyful child melancholy and grave. He took its ancient ladies with their biblical-sounding names for patriarchs and phantoms. Hugo catalogues the habitués: marquises and viscounts, the Chevalier de Port-de-Guy who had been chained in the galleys at Toulon in 1793 gathering guillotined bodies, a bailiff who had humbled the dancer Guimard, abbés and preachers, the Pope's Nuncio, two cardinals (one a merry billiards player), five peers of France including the Duc de Valentinois, Prince of Monaco. Over this feudal salon a bourgeois, Gillenormand, reigned.

There taste was haughty, speech barely a breath, and the vocabulary consisted of 'conserve' and 'conservation'; the masters were embalmed, the servants stuffed with straw. They spoke of the king in the third person because 'Your Majesty' had been soiled by the usurper, and held that the time since Coblentz had not existed. What did they do there? They were ultra: to be ultra is to attack the sceptre in the name of the throne, to find the Pope not papish enough and the king not royal enough, to be so strongly for as to be against.

Hugo sketches the six years from 1814 to 1820, when returned émigrés scorned the nobility of the Empire and called Bonaparte Scapin, a world now vanished beneath two revolutions; from 1818 the doctrinarians appeared, Royalists ashamed of being so, who argued that France should accept the whole of its history. He adds that he recalls this world without bitterness, since it touches the memory of his mother.

Marius was handed from his prudish aunt to a pedantic classical tutor, went through college and entered the law school. He was a fanatical and severe Royalist, did not much love his cynical grandfather, and was gloomy about his father: a cold and ardent, noble, proud, religious lad, dignified to harshness and pure to shyness.

title: End of the Brigand
summary: In 1827 Gillenormand sends the seventeen-year-old Marius to Vernon to see his dying father. Marius arrives to find the colonel dead, having risen in delirium to go and meet the son who had not come. Marius feels only a stranger's grief, keeps a note in which the colonel bequeaths him his title of baron and bids him do good to a sergeant named Thénardier who saved his life at Waterloo, and forgets his father in three days.
details: When Marius finished his classical studies Gillenormand left society for the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, with Nicolette and Basque for servants. In 1827, when Marius was seventeen, his grandfather told him he would leave for Vernon the next day to see his father, who was ill and asked for him. Marius was shaken; he had thought of everything except this, and, convinced the father who had abandoned him did not love him, he did not love him. Neither thought to take the night coach that would have got him there by morning.

At twilight the next day Marius asked in Vernon for 'M. Pontmercy's house', refusing him his titles as the Restoration did. A weeping woman opened the door and told him his father no longer expected him. In a candlelit room on the ground floor lay the colonel in his shirt, dead on the floor, with a doctor and the praying curé beside him. Struck by brain fever three days before, he had written for his son; that very evening, delirious, he had risen crying, 'My son is not coming! I shall go to meet him!', run into the antechamber and fallen dead. A large tear still stood on his cheek: his son's delay.

Marius looked for the first time at that scarred, heroic face and felt only the chill he would have felt before any dead stranger. Ashamed of his own coldness amid the others' grief, he let his hat fall to feign being overcome, and despised himself for it. The colonel left nothing; the sale of his furniture barely paid for his burial. The servant handed Marius a paper in the colonel's hand: the Emperor had made him a baron at Waterloo, and since the Restoration disputed the title, his son should take and bear it and would be worthy of it. Below, the colonel added that a sergeant named Thénardier had saved his life at Waterloo and now kept an inn near Paris, at Chelles or Montfermeil; if his son met him, he should do him all the good he could.

Marius kept the paper out of a vague respect for death. Gillenormand sold the colonel's sword and uniform to an old-clothes dealer; neighbours pillaged the rare flowers and the garden went to nettles. Marius stayed forty-eight hours, returned to his law studies and put on crape; in two days the colonel was buried and in three forgotten.

title: The Utility of Going to Mass, in Order to Become a Revolutionist
summary: At Saint-Sulpice an old churchwarden, M. Mabeuf, reclaims his chair from Marius and explains why he prizes it: from there he watched a poor father come secretly for ten years to gaze at the son he was forbidden to see. The father was Colonel Pontmercy. Shaken, Marius asks his grandfather for leave to go 'hunting'.
details: One Sunday at Saint-Sulpice, Marius absent-mindedly knelt on a chair bearing the name 'Monsieur Mabeuf, warden'. An old man claimed it, and after mass apologised and explained his attachment to the spot. From that chair he had watched, for ten years, a poor brave father who came every two or three months to see his child at mass, the only way left him since the family forbade it; he hid behind a pillar, gazed at the boy and wept. A father-in-law and a rich aunt had threatened to disinherit the child if the father saw him; the man had sacrificed himself for his son's future over political opinions. He had been one of Bonaparte's colonels, lived at Vernon where the warden's brother was curé, and was called something like Pontmarie or Montpercy.
'Pontmercy,' said Marius, turning pale: 'he was my father.' The old warden clasped his hands and told him he could say he had had a father who loved him dearly. Marius saw him home.
Next day Marius asked his grandfather's leave for a three-day hunting party with friends. 'Four!' said Gillenormand, and whispered to his daughter with a wink that it was some love affair.

title: The Consequences of Having Met a Warden
summary: Marius returns from his three days and devours the history of the Republic and the Empire, coming to adore the father he had neglected and, after a long inner struggle, Napoleon too. He turns republican and Bonapartist, orders cards reading 'Le Baron Marius Pontmercy', cools towards his grandfather, searches Montfermeil in vain for Thénardier, and wears something on a black ribbon round his neck.
details: Where Marius went on his absence Hugo defers. On his return he went straight to the law-school library for the Moniteur, then read every history, memoir and bulletin of the Republic and Empire. Finding his father's name in the bulletins of the grand army gave him a week's fever. He visited generals under whom Georges Pontmercy had served and went back to the warden Mabeuf, who told him of the colonel's flowers and solitude at Vernon. Marius came to know the rare, sweet, sublime man his father had been, and was on the high road to adoring him, while his grandfather, seeing him vanish from meals, chuckled that it was an affair of passion.

His ideas changed with his heart. The Republic and Empire, which had been a guillotine and a sword in the dark, now appeared as stars and a rising sun; he judged that all this had been good, and understood that he had known neither his country nor his father. He was tormented by remorse that his love could now be spoken only to a tomb. From rehabilitating his father he passed, with more labour, to rehabilitating Napoleon, whom the party of 1814 had taught him to see as the Corsican Ogre; one night, reading the bulletins at his open window under the stars, hearing in imagination the drums and cavalry of the Empire, he leapt up, stretched his arms into the dark and cried, 'Long live the Emperor!' Napoleon became for him the incarnation of France, the man-people. Hugo notes that, like all converts, he went too far, admitting force along with genius.

Having shed his Bourbon and ultra skin and become a democrat and republican, he ordered a hundred cards engraved 'Le Baron Marius Pontmercy', and, knowing no one to leave them with, kept them in his pocket. As he drew nearer his father he receded from his grandfather, whose frivolity had always jarred on him and who, he now reflected, had torn him from the colonel; pity for the father brought him near to aversion for the grandfather, though outwardly he only grew colder and rarer at home. His aunt wondered where he went. On one brief trip he went to Montfermeil to find the sergeant of Waterloo, the innkeeper Thénardier, but the inn had failed and closed and no one knew where he had gone. The family thought they saw something hanging from his neck on a black ribbon.

title: Some Petticoat
summary: Aunt Gillenormand, convinced Marius's absences hide a love affair, pays her favourite, Lieutenant Théodule, ten louis to shadow him on the diligence. At Vernon Théodule follows Marius, who buys flowers and goes behind the church, and finds him sobbing on a grave marked 'Colonel Baron Pontmercy'. The 'lass' was a grave.
details: Lieutenant Théodule Gillenormand, a great-grand-nephew on the paternal side, was a fine lancer officer with a lady's waist who rarely visited Paris; Marius had never met him. He was the aunt's favourite because she never saw him. One morning, puzzled and faintly scandalised that Marius had again asked leave to go away that evening, Mademoiselle Gillenormand was embroidering cartwheels when Théodule walked in, passing through Paris as his regiment moved from Melun to Gaillon. She gave him ten louis and begged him to stay; he had to leave that night.

Théodule mentioned that, booking his seat in the diligence, he had seen the name Marius Pontmercy on the card of a traveller in the imperial, bound for Andelys by way of Vernon. The aunt seized on it: Marius absents himself, travels, sleeps out, and nobody knows why. 'Some petticoat or other,' said Théodule; 'a lass.' Since the cousins did not know each other, she asked him to follow Marius, get a sight of the girl and write to amuse the grandfather. Touched by the ten louis, he agreed, telling himself he had become a duenna.

He slept all night in the coupé and woke at Vernon, where he was to change coaches, laughing at the commission. Then Marius climbed down from the imperial, bought the finest flowers from a peasant girl's basket and walked, seeing nothing, towards the church. Now curious on his own account, Théodule followed, expecting a rendezvous spiced with mass. Marius skirted the apse and vanished round a corner; Théodule crept after him and stopped in amazement. Marius was kneeling in the grass on a grave, his bouquet strewn on it, sobbing, before a black wooden cross lettered in white: Colonel Baron Pontmercy.

title: Marble Against Granite
summary: Théodule writes nothing, but back in Paris Gillenormand finds the medallion Marius wore: inside is the colonel's note bequeathing his title, and in the coat the cards of 'Le Baron Marius Pontmercy'. The confrontation ends with Marius shouting 'Down with the Bourbons!' and the grandfather ordering him out. Marius leaves with thirty francs, and the medallion is lost on the stairs.
details: The grave was where Marius had gone each time his grandfather said he was 'sleeping out'. Théodule, abashed before the tomb and the colonel, retreated with something like a military salute and decided not to write to his aunt. Nothing might have come of it had the scene not had an immediate echo in Paris. Returning on the third morning, Marius ran up to his room, threw off his greatcoat and the black ribbon from his neck and went straight out to the swimming-school. Gillenormand, who had hurried upstairs to embrace and question him, found only the coat and ribbon on the bed and said, 'I like this better.'

He carried his trophies triumphantly to the salon where his daughter sat embroidering: here was the romance, the portrait worn on the heart. The black shagreen case held only a folded paper, which he took for a love-letter, and the aunt put on her spectacles. They read the colonel's words: the Emperor had made him a baron at Waterloo, and his son should take the title and be worthy of it. Father and daughter felt chilled as by a death's-head. 'It is the slasher's handwriting,' Gillenormand murmured. Then a packet of blue paper fell from the coat pocket: Marius's hundred cards, 'Le Baron Marius Pontmercy'. Gillenormand rang for Nicolette, flung coat, ribbon and case on the floor and told her to carry the duds away. An hour of silence followed.

When Marius came in, his grandfather, holding one of the cards, mockingly congratulated him on being a baron. 'It means that I am the son of my father,' Marius replied. 'I am your father,' said Gillenormand harshly. Marius answered that his father was a humble and heroic man who had served the Republic and France gloriously for twenty-five years, had taken two flags and twenty wounds, and had died forgotten, having made only one mistake, to love two ingrates too well, his country and his son. At the word 'republic' the old man sprang up and exploded: he did not know and would not know what Marius's father was, but all who served B-u-o-naparte were brigands, traitors and cowards, and Marius was no more a baron than his slipper.

Torn between a sacred grave and hoary locks, unable to insult his grandfather or leave his father unavenged, Marius stood staggering, then cried in a voice of thunder, 'Down with the Bourbons, and that great hog of a Louis XVIII!' (dead these four years). Gillenormand turned white, bowed solemnly to a bust of the Duc de Berry, paced the room twice in silence, told his daughter with an almost calm smile that a baron like this gentleman and a bourgeois like himself could not stay under one roof, then pointed at Marius and shouted, 'Be off!' Marius left. Next day Gillenormand ordered his daughter to send 'that blood-drinker' sixty pistoles every six months and never to speak his name, and addressed her as 'you' for three months. Nicolette had dropped the medallion on the dark attic stairs; it was never found, and Marius, who knew the lines by heart, was convinced 'Monsieur Gillenormand' had burned his father's testament. He went off in a hackney-coach toward the Latin quarter with thirty francs, his watch and a few clothes.

title: A Group Which Barely Missed Becoming Historic
summary: Hugo introduces the Friends of the A.B.C., a small secret society of students meeting in the back room of the Café Musain, and draws portraits of its members: Enjolras, Combeferre, Jean Prouvaire, Feuilly, Courfeyrac, Bahorel, Bossuet (Lesgle), Joly and the sceptic Grantaire.
details: A revolutionary quiver was in the air of that time; Royalists were becoming liberals and liberals democrats, and people adored both Napoleon and liberty. Among the small secret groups forming in Paris was the society of the Friends of the A.B.C., ostensibly for the education of children, really for the elevation of man: a pun on the Abaissé, the debased, the people. They met near the markets in a wine-shop called Corinthe and, more often, in a back room of the Café Musain near the Panthéon, reached by a long corridor, with a private stair to the Rue des Grès and a map of Republican France on the wall. They were mostly students from the South, on good terms with working men.

Enjolras, an only son and wealthy, is angelically handsome and capable of being terrible, a priest and soldier of the ideal, twenty-two looking seventeen, with one passion, the right, and no eye for women; he would have been Saint-Just in the Convention. Combeferre represents the philosophy of the Revolution beside Enjolras's logic: broader, gentler, a Polytechnic graduate who reads everything, believes in railways and balloons, and prefers the dawn to the conflagration; Enjolras is a chief, Combeferre a guide. Jean Prouvaire, who spells his name Jehan, is softer still: a shy, badly dressed, erudite poet in love, who studies social questions by day and planets by night, and is intrepid. Feuilly is a fan-maker, an orphan earning three francs a day, self-taught, who has adopted the oppressed peoples of the world and is inexhaustible on the partition of Poland.

Courfeyrac has dropped the particle from his father's name; he has the sparkling youth of Tholomyès in 1817, but with a paladin where Tholomyès had a district attorney; he is the centre of the group, its warmth. Bahorel, a cheerful brawler in his eleventh year as a law student, spends his peasant parents' money doing nothing, loves a quarrel less than an uprising and an uprising less than a revolution, and links the group to others. Lesgle or Laigle of Meaux, the one bald member, signs himself Légle (de Meaux) and is nicknamed Bossuet: a gay and spectacularly unlucky fellow who has lost his inheritance and lodges wherever he can, most often with Joly. Joly is a medical student and hypochondriac who sleeps with his head to the south and feels his pulse in thunderstorms, otherwise the gayest of all.

All share one religion, Progress, and are the direct sons of '89. Among them sits one sceptic, Grantaire, who signs himself with the rebus R: a drinker, boxer and connoisseur of every café in Paris, inordinately ugly, who believes in nothing, mocks every devotion and hums drinking-songs. His one fanaticism is a man, Enjolras, whom he admires, loves and venerates as his opposite; his shapeless ideas lean on that firmness like a spine. Enjolras disdains the drunkard and treats him harshly; Grantaire, rebuffed and always returning, says of him, 'What fine marble!'

title: Blondeau’s Funeral Oration by Bossuet
summary: Lounging outside the Café Musain, Laigle de Meaux hails a cab carrying Marius Pontmercy and explains that he answered to Marius's name at roll-call, saving him from being struck off and getting himself struck off instead. Courfeyrac comes out and takes the homeless Marius to lodge with him at the hôtel de la Porte-Saint-Jacques.
details: On the afternoon that followed Marius's expulsion, Laigle de Meaux leaned against the doorpost of the Café Musain, musing on a misadventure at the law school two days earlier. A cab passed at a walk carrying a young man and a bag labelled Marius Pontmercy. Laigle hailed him. Marius, fresh from his grandfather's and in no mood for jokes, did not know him; Laigle did not know Marius either, but had been looking for him.

He told his story. Entering the lecture by chance, he had heard the professor Blondeau, who delighted in scenting out absentees, call 'Marius Pontmercy' three times; at the third call, when the name would have been erased and sixty francs lost, Laigle, out of compassion for an honourable idler who did not attend, answered 'Present!' Blondeau then skipped to the letter L and called 'Laigle'; Laigle answered 'Present!' again, and Blondeau, observing that if he was Pontmercy he was not Laigle, crossed him off instead. Laigle delivered a mock funeral oration on Blondeau and declared himself delighted: the erasure saved him from becoming a lawyer.

Asked where he lived so that Laigle might call to thank him, Marius answered, 'In this cab,' which he had hired by the hour and did not know how to get rid of. Courfeyrac came out of the café at that moment and said, 'Come to my place.' Laigle claimed priority but admitted he had no home; Courfeyrac told 'Bossuet' to hold his tongue, and Laigle explained the metaphor to a puzzled Marius. That evening Marius was installed beside Courfeyrac in a room at the hôtel de la Porte-Saint-Jacques.

title: Marius’ Astonishments
summary: Marius befriends Courfeyrac, declares himself a 'democrat-Bonapartist' and is introduced at the Café Musain as 'a pupil'. The irreverent, free-ranging talk of the Friends of the A.B.C. unsettles the convictions he thought he had fixed; none of them says 'the Emperor'.
details: Within days Marius and Courfeyrac were friends; Courfeyrac asked no questions, since at that age faces say everything. One morning he asked Marius his political opinions. 'A democrat-Bonapartist,' said Marius. 'The grey hue of a reassured rat,' said Courfeyrac, and next day took him to the Café Musain to give him, as he whispered, his entry to the revolution, presenting him to the Friends of the A.B.C. with the single word 'A pupil'.

Marius had fallen into a wasps' nest of wits. Solitary and used to soliloquy, he was buffeted by these free minds talking of philosophy, art, history and religion in unexpected ways, and, having thought himself fixed since exchanging his grandfather's opinions for his father's, he uneasily suspected he was not. Nothing seemed sacred to them. When Bahorel cried down classical tragedy, Combeferre defended its right to exist as the duck exists beside the bird. In the Rue Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Courfeyrac joked about Rousseau and Thérèse and their children sent to the foundlings, and Enjolras cut him short: Rousseau denied his children, perhaps, but he adopted the people.

Not one of them said 'the Emperor'. Jean Prouvaire alone sometimes said Napoleon; the others said Bonaparte, and Enjolras pronounced it Buonaparte. Marius was vaguely surprised: the beginning of wisdom.

title: The Back Room of the Café Musain
summary: An evening of uproar in the back room: Grantaire, drunk, harangues on vanity and the worthlessness of all nations; Bossuet talks law; two men draft a vaudeville; Joly and Bahorel discuss mistresses; Prouvaire defends the pagan gods; Courfeyrac denounces kings and the Charter and flings a copy of it into the fire.
details: Nearly all the Friends of the A.B.C. were in the back room that evening, talking loudly and at random while Enjolras and Marius kept silent. Only Louison the dishwasher ever passed through. Grantaire, thoroughly drunk, held one corner, demanding drink and declaring life a hideous invention, everything vanity dressed in big words, every virtue bordering on a vice, all history plagiarism, victory stupid and glory a matter of convincing. He ran through the nations one by one, Greece, England, America, Germany, Italy, Russia, Asia, finding each absurd, concluded that Paris carried the day since even its ragpickers were sybarites, and ended by catching at Louison as his Cleopatra. When Bossuet tried to quiet him he grew worse, pronouncing man a failure and woman a rhyme for infamous.

Bossuet, meanwhile, was deep in a point of Norman customary law; two heads bent over paper were inventing names for a vaudeville; a man of thirty was warning a youth of eighteen that his duelling adversary was a fine left-handed swordsman. Joly and Bahorel played dominoes and talked of love: Bahorel on the dangers of a mistress who laughs, Joly sighing over his sulking Musichetta and being advised to buy elegant trousers. In another corner Jean Prouvaire, roused from his timidity, championed Olympus against Christian mythology, insisting Jupiter might not be dead and Pan might still breathe into the willows.

In the last corner they talked politics. Combeferre weakly defended the Charter; Courfeyrac attacked it, brandishing a copy of the Touquet Charter. He wanted no kings, if only because they are expensive, and no charter granted from above, which is a mask with a lie beneath it and an Article 14 to snatch back what it gives. It was winter and a fire was burning; he crumpled the Charter and flung it in. 'The charter metamorphosed into flame,' said Combeferre, watching it burn.

title: Enlargement of Horizon
summary: Bossuet's chance mention of Waterloo, Courfeyrac's remark on Bonaparte's fatal number 18 and Enjolras's word 'crime' provoke Marius into a passionate defence of Napoleon and the Empire. Combeferre answers with two words, 'To be free,' and leaves singing of a mother preferred to Caesar; Enjolras tells Marius, 'My mother is the Republic.'
details: In the midst of the crossfire of jokes, Bossuet ended some remark to Combeferre with the date '18 June 1815, Waterloo'. Marius, elbows on a table beside a glass of water, looked up. Courfeyrac observed that 18 was Bonaparte's fatal number, Brumaire at the beginning, June at the end. Enjolras, silent till then, called it the crime and the expiation. That word was more than Marius could bear. He went to the map of France on the wall, laid his finger on the inset of Corsica and said: a little island which has made France very great.

A chill fell on the room. Enjolras, gazing at nothing, replied that France needed no Corsica to be great; France is great because she is France. Marius turned on him and poured out his confession of faith: he heard them say Buonaparte like Royalists, and his grandfather did worse; where was their enthusiasm, and whom did they admire if not the Emperor? He had everything: codes like Justinian, dictation like Caesar, bulletins that were Iliads; he taught emperors majesty at Tilsit and answered Laplace at the Academy, and then Europe trembled, the armies moved, and he rose on the horizon with a blazing brand, the archangel of war. What a destiny for a nation to be the Empire of such an Emperor, to make kings of grenadiers, to hurl into history words like Marengo, Arcola, Austerlitz, to conquer the world twice, by conquest and by dazzlement; what greater thing is there?

'To be free,' said Combeferre. The cold, simple words went through Marius's epic like a blade and he lowered his head; when he looked up, Combeferre had gone and all the others but Enjolras had followed him. As Marius gathered his thoughts to argue, they heard Combeferre on the stairs singing a song about a man who, offered glory and war by Caesar at the price of leaving his mother, would hand back the sceptre and chariot: 'I love my mother better.' Marius repeated mechanically, 'My mother?' and felt Enjolras's hand on his shoulder. 'Citizen,' said Enjolras, 'my mother is the Republic.'

title: Res Angusta
summary: Shaken and isolated, Marius stops going to the Café Musain. The hotel demands payment; with Courfeyrac's help he sells his clothes and gold watch, pays the bill and has ten francs left. His aunt finds him and sends sixty pistoles, which he returns; he leaves the hotel to avoid debt.
details: The evening left Marius profoundly shaken, like earth torn open for the seed. He had barely acquired a faith and already doubted it; standing between two religions, one not yet left and one not yet entered, he feared that each step toward his friends was a step away from his father. Daring to his grandfather, behind the times to his friends, he felt doubly isolated and ceased to go to the Café Musain.

Reality elbowed him. One morning the hotel-keeper, who had let him stay on Courfeyrac's word, demanded his money. Marius told Courfeyrac what he had never mentioned: that he was alone in the world without relatives. Courfeyrac questioned him: fifteen francs, no debts wanted, a frock-coat and trousers to sell, a gold watch, no English or German, which might have earned him translating work for a publisher friend. 'I will learn English and German,' said Marius, and live meanwhile on his clothes and watch. The clothes fetched twenty francs, the watch forty-five; with his fifteen that made eighty. The hotel bill was seventy, leaving ten francs, as Courfeyrac drily computed, five for English and five for German.

Aunt Gillenormand, good-hearted at bottom, had found out where he lived and sent sixty pistoles, six hundred francs in gold, in a sealed box. Marius sent the money back with a respectful letter saying he could supply all his needs; at that moment he had three francs. She did not tell her father of the refusal, for fear of his rage. Marius left the hotel rather than run into debt.

title: Marius Indigent
summary: Marius learns the bitter diet of poverty: days without bread, a cutlet eked out over three days, a borrowed coat turned so that it is green and worn only after dark to pass for black. He returns his aunt's money each time, is admitted as a lawyer and writes coldly to tell his grandfather, who tears up the letter.
details: Life became hard. Marius ate what the French call the mad cow: days without bread, nights without sleep, evenings without a candle, a door locked for unpaid rent, the sneers of porters and cook-shop men. At the age when a young man most needs his pride he was jeered at for his clothes and ridiculed for his poverty. Hugo calls it the crucible from which the feeble emerge base and the strong sublime; there are obscure heroes in the petty battles of destitution.

There came a time when Marius swept his own landing, bought a sou's worth of Brie and slipped into the baker's at dusk as if stealing his loaf. An awkward young man with books under his arm would bow to the butcher's wife, buy a mutton cutlet for six or seven sous, and live on it for three days: meat the first day, fat the second, the bone the third. His aunt sent the sixty pistoles again and again; he returned them every time. Still in mourning for his father, he found his black clothes wearing out; Courfeyrac gave him an old coat which Marius had turned for thirty sous, but it was green, so he went out only after nightfall, which made it black: he clothed himself with the night.

In spite of everything he was admitted to practise as a lawyer, nominally living in Courfeyrac's room, whose law books served as the required library. He informed his grandfather in a cold, submissive letter. Gillenormand read it trembling, tore it in four and threw it in the wastebasket; days later his daughter overheard him telling himself that a man cannot be a baron and a lawyer at the same time.

title: Marius Poor
summary: Marius settles into a frugal order: seven hundred francs a year from hack work for a publisher, a fireless room in the Gorbeau house, dinner at Rousseau's for sixteen sous, never a debt. Beside his father's name he venerates that of Thénardier, the sergeant of Waterloo, whom he has searched for in vain for three years.
details: Wretchedness ends by becoming bearable. Through Courfeyrac's publisher friend Marius, having learned English and German, earned about seven hundred francs a year drawing up prospectuses, translating newspapers and compiling biographies. He rented for thirty francs a year a fireless room called a cabinet in the Gorbeau house, paid the old principal tenant three francs a month to sweep it and bring hot water, an egg and a roll each morning, and dined at six at Rousseau's in the Rue Saint-Jacques, 'Rousseau the Aquatic', on a six-sou plate of meat, vegetables, dessert and bread for sixteen sous, drinking water and winning a smile from Madame Rousseau. Food, rent, service, clothes, linen and washing came to about six hundred and fifty francs; he was rich, and sometimes lent ten francs to a friend. He had two black suits, one old and one new, and three shirts, always ragged, so he buttoned his coat to the chin.

It had taken hard years to reach this flourishing state, and he had never once contracted a debt, which he regarded as the beginning of slavery; rather than borrow he went without food. Fearing that lowered fortunes might lower his soul, he kept a jealous watch on his pride and was timid to the point of rudeness. A secret inner force upheld him: the soul is the only bird that bears up its own cage.

Beside his father's name another was graven in his heart, Thénardier, the intrepid sergeant who had carried the colonel out of the bullets at Waterloo. Marius worshipped him on a lesser altar beside his father, the more tenderly because he had learned at Montfermeil of the innkeeper's ruin and bankruptcy. For three years he had scoured Chelles, Bondy, Gournay, Nogent and Lagny with his small savings, finding no trace; Thénardier was thought to have gone abroad, and even his creditors could not find him. It was the one debt his father had left him, and his sweetest dream was to find Thénardier, rescue him from misery and say, 'You do not know me; well, I know you! Dispose of me!'

title: Marius Grown Up
summary: Three years after leaving home, Marius is twenty. Unknown to him, Gillenormand secretly pines for his grandson while refusing to take a step; Marius, for his part, is glad to suffer for his father's sake, inclines too much to contemplation, declines a publisher's offer of fifteen hundred francs, and has two friends, Courfeyrac and the old churchwarden M. Mabeuf.
details: Marius was twenty and had been gone three years; neither side had sought the other. He was mistaken about his grandfather's heart. There is no grandfather who does not adore his grandson, and Gillenormand, who idolised Marius with boxes on the ear, felt a black void when he left. He had expected the 'Jacobin' to return; years passed and he did not. Asked whether he would turn him out again, his pride said yes and his old head sadly shook no. He never inquired about Marius but thought of him incessantly, grew more retired, and said sometimes, 'Oh! if he only would return, what a good box on the ear I would give him!' To busybodies he answered with a sigh that Monsieur le Baron de Pontmercy was pettifogging in some corner. The aunt thought too little to love much and cared more for her cat or parakeet.

Marius, meanwhile, applauded himself. Misfortune had removed his bitterness; he thought of Gillenormand kindly but would accept nothing from the man who had been unkind to his father. He was happy to suffer: it was an expiation for his own impious indifference, the only way to approach and resemble his father, to be brave before indigence as the colonel had been before the enemy, and surely what 'He will be worthy of it' had meant. He had left a child and was now a man. Hugo praises the poverty of youth that turns the will to effort and the soul to aspiration, giving the poor young man work, which makes him free, and thought, which makes him dignified.

Yet Marius inclined too far toward contemplation; having secured his living he worked as little as possible and gave whole days to reverie, not seeing that this was becoming a form of idleness. Though a lawyer, he did not plead. A publisher, Magimel, offered to lodge him and pay fifteen hundred francs a year for regular work; he refused rather than lose his liberty. He had not entered decisively into Enjolras's group, though they remained friends. He had two friends, one young, Courfeyrac, and one old, M. Mabeuf, to whom he owed the revolution in himself and the knowledge of his father: 'He operated on me for a cataract.' Mabeuf had been the candle, not the hand that carried it, and understood nothing of Marius's politics.

title: M. Mabeuf
summary: Portrait of M. Mabeuf, the gentle old churchwarden who loves only plants and old books, lives on his Flora of the Environs of Cauteretz with his housekeeper Mother Plutarque, and after 1830 slides into poverty, losing ten thousand francs to a notary's failure and moving to a cottage in the village of Austerlitz near the Salpêtrière.
details: When Mabeuf told Marius he approved of political opinions, he meant it: he approved them all, provided they left him in peace. He was neither Royalist nor Bonapartist but a bouquinist, a collector of old books, and could not see why men hated each other over charters and republics when there were mosses, shrubs and folios to look at. He had bred seedling pears and perhaps originated the October Mirabelle; what the colonel did for flowers he did for fruits. He went to mass from gentleness, loving men's faces but hating their noise, and had chosen the career of warden to be something in the State. He had never loved a woman as much as a tulip bulb; asked if he had ever married, he said he had forgotten. He had published a Flora of the Environs of Cauteretz with coloured plates which sold well and brought in about two thousand francs a year, nearly his whole fortune, and had patiently formed a precious collection of rare books. The sight of a gun chilled his blood. His only friend was an old bookseller of the Porte-Saint-Jacques named Royal, and his dream was to naturalise indigo in France.

His housekeeper, an innocent old spinster with a moustache and a cat called Sultan, whom he nicknamed Mother Plutarque, could read and spent Sundays counting her linen. Mabeuf took to Marius because the young man's gentleness warmed his age without startling his timidity, and when Marius came saturated with his father's battles, Mabeuf talked of the hero from the point of view of flowers.

About 1830 his brother the curé died, a notary's failure swallowed the ten thousand francs that was all he and his brother had, and the July Revolution brought a crisis in publishing; the first thing not to sell in hard times is a Flora, and purchasers stopped coming. He gave up the Rue Mésières and his wardenship, sold his prints rather than his books, tried a house in the Rue Montparnasse which was too dear and too near a shooting-gallery, and settled for fifty crowns a year in a thatched cottage with a garden and well in the village of Austerlitz near the Salpêtrière, a name he found disagreeably warlike. He hung his herbariums himself, dug all day and told the melancholy Mother Plutarque, 'We have the indigo!' Only Royal and Marius were admitted there.

Absorbed minds, Hugo observes, are slow to notice their own ruin; Mabeuf remained serene as his hopes went out one by one, like a clock that keeps going after the key is lost. His pleasures were cheap and unexpected: hearing Mother Plutarque read aloud a romance in which 'the beauty pouted, and the dragoon', he drifted into a reverie about Buddha converting the dragon and pronounced it a beautiful book.

title: Poverty a Good Neighbor for Misery
summary: Marius, known at the Gorbeau house only as M. Marius, takes long solitary walks, visits his father's old generals when the weather lets him arrive with clean boots, and finds his political fever cooled into sympathies after 1830. In mid-1831 he learns that his neighbours, the wretched Jondrettes, are to be evicted for twenty francs of rent, and secretly pays it, adding five francs for them.
details: Marius liked the candid old man who was sliding toward indigence without becoming melancholy, and saw him, like Courfeyrac, rarely, twice a month at most. His pleasure was to walk alone on the outer boulevards, the Champ-de-Mars or the quieter alleys of the Luxembourg, spending half a day watching a market garden or a horse at a waterwheel; passers-by found his look suspicious. On one such stroll he had found the Gorbeau house and taken a room there for its isolation and cheapness; there he was known only as M. Marius. Some of his father's old generals and comrades, Comte Pajol, General Bellavesne, General Fririon, invited him to their evenings; he went, in his new coat, only on freezing days, since he could not afford a carriage and would not arrive with boots other than mirrors. A drawing-room, he said, forgives everything but your shoes.

Reverie had dissolved his political fevers, and the Revolution of 1830 had calmed them. He held the same opinions, tempered; more exactly, he had no longer opinions but sympathies. His party was humanity; within humanity France, within the nation the people, within the people woman. He now preferred an idea to a deed and Job to Marengo, and from gazing at the sky over the boulevards had come to look at little else, while multiplying plans and scaffoldings for the future. Hugo adds that a man is better judged by his dreams than by his thoughts, and Marius's soul, seen within, would have dazzled by its purity.

Towards the middle of 1831 the old woman who served him told him that his neighbours, the wretched Jondrette family, were being turned out for owing two quarters' rent, twenty francs. Marius, who spent his days outside and hardly knew he had neighbours, had thirty francs saved in a drawer. He gave her twenty-five: pay for the poor people, give them five francs, and do not tell them it was I.

title: The Substitute
summary: Aunt Gillenormand tries to install Théodule, now garrisoned in Paris, as a substitute grandson. Enraged by a newspaper report that students will 'deliberate' at the Panthéon, the old man rails for pages against the young, the republic, romanticism and his absent Marius while the lancer dutifully agrees with everything, until Gillenormand turns on him: 'You are a fool.'
details: Théodule's regiment came to Paris, and the aunt, having once used him to spy on Marius, now planned to have him replace Marius in the old man's affections: for Marius, read Théodule. She announced that his grandnephew would call. 'Who's Théodule?' said Gillenormand, and returned to his Royalist paper, which reported that the law and medical students would assemble at midday on the Place du Panthéon to deliberate on the National Guard's artillery. He thought at once of Marius, who was a student and would surely go.

Théodule entered in plain clothes, calculating that the old druid had not sunk all his money in an annuity, and was told by his aunt in a whisper to approve of everything. He stammered 'Good day, uncle'; Gillenormand told him to sit down and forgot him, pacing with his hands in his fobs and talking aloud. Brats scarcely weaned were to deliberate in the open air; the Republicans and the galley-slaves were one nose and one handkerchief. He turned to the absent Marius: why had he left his house to become a Republican, a Carbonaro? The people wanted no republic; the nineteenth century was poison; the young let their beards grow, called themselves romantics, ran to Hernani, dressed like stablemen, were afraid of women and reconstructed Europe while ogling laundresses' ankles. 'That is true,' 'You are right, uncle,' 'That is evident,' said Théodule at intervals, and once ventured that there should be no newspaper but the Moniteur and no book but the Army List.

Gillenormand went on, cursing newspapers, the Odéon arcades where students read them, Sieyès the regicide turned senator, and the whole dream of progress, humanity and revolution, which he denounced as madness, crime and monster. 'Parbleu!' cried the lieutenant, 'that is wonderfully true.' The old man stopped in mid-gesture, wheeled round, stared him in the eyes and said: 'You are a fool.'

title: The Sobriquet: Mode of Formation of Family Names
summary: Marius, handsome but shy of women, has for a year noticed in a quiet alley of the Luxembourg a white-haired man of about sixty and a plain, thin girl of thirteen or fourteen who sit on the same bench daily. Courfeyrac has nicknamed them Monsieur Leblanc and Mademoiselle Lanoire; Marius finds the man agreeable and the girl insipid.
details: Marius was now a handsome young man with thick black hair, a lofty brow and a charming smile that softened a severe face, reserved and cold in manner. In his worst poverty he had thought girls turned to laugh at his clothes, when they turned because they dreamed of him, and the misunderstanding had made him shy; he fled them all. Courfeyrac, who called him Monsieur l'Abbé, advised him to read fewer books and look at the lasses, which only made Marius avoid women, and Courfeyrac, for a week.

Two women he did not flee, because he never thought of them as women: the bearded old woman who swept his room, and a sort of little girl he saw constantly and never looked at. For more than a year, in the Luxembourg walk along the Pépinière, at its loneliest end on the Rue de l'Ouest side, he had found a man and a very young girl almost always on the same bench. The man seemed about sixty, sad, serious, with the robust and weary look of a retired officer, a kindly but unapproachable air, very white hair, and a blue coat, a broad-brimmed hat and a coarse but dazzling white shirt. The girl, when she first came, was thirteen or fourteen, thin almost to plainness, awkward, with a promise of fine eyes raised with a displeasing assurance, in a badly cut black merino gown like a convent schoolgirl's. They looked like father and daughter and talked together peacefully, she chattering, he saying little and gazing at her with ineffable paternity.

Marius had the mechanical habit of walking the alley's length five or six times, passing the bench each time, five or six days a week, without a greeting on either side. The couple had caught the attention of the few students who used that walk; Courfeyrac, finding the girl homely, had fled, naming the daughter Mademoiselle Lanoire for her dress and the father Monsieur Leblanc for his hair, and the nickname stuck for want of any other. Hugo adopts it too. Through the first year Marius saw them nearly every day and found the man to his taste and the girl insipid.

title: Lux Facta Est
summary: After six months away from the alley, Marius returns one summer morning to find the same man with what seems another girl: the awkward child has become a beautiful, elegantly dressed young woman of fifteen. She glances at him indifferently and he passes on, thinking of other things.
details: In the second year, at the point the story has now reached, Marius's habit of the Luxembourg lapsed for nearly six months without his quite knowing why. One serene summer morning, in joyous mood, he went straight to his alley and saw the familiar couple on their bench. The man was the same; the girl, it seemed to him, was not. She was now a tall and beautiful creature at the exact moment when a woman's lines still carry a child's grace, 'fifteen years': brown hair threaded with gold, a marble brow, rose-leaf cheeks, an exquisite mouth, and a nose that was not handsome but pretty, the Parisian nose. Her eyes were lowered; he saw only long chestnut lashes.

He thought for a moment she must be a sister of the earlier girl, but on his second pass recognised her: in six months the little girl had become a young maiden, as trees flower in three April days. She had grown and been idealised, and taste had come with beauty. Gone were the felt hat, merino gown and red hands; she wore black damask with a cape of the same, a white crape bonnet, white gloves, a parasol with a carved Chinese ivory handle and silk shoes, and exhaled a youthful perfume. The man was as usual.

The second time Marius approached, she raised eyes of deep celestial blue that held as yet only a child's glance, looked at him as indifferently as at a brat under the sycamores or a marble vase, and he walked on thinking of something else. In the following days he found 'the father and daughter' there as usual and paid them no more attention now that she was beautiful than when she was plain.

title: Effect of the Spring
summary: On a warm, luminous day in the Luxembourg, the girl raises her eyes as Marius passes and their glances meet; something strange flashes in hers. That evening he notices for the first time how shabbily he has been dressing for his walks.
details: One day the air was warm, the Luxembourg flooded with light and shade, sparrows twittering in the chestnuts, and Marius, his soul open to nature and thinking of nothing, passed the bench; the young girl raised her eyes to him and the two glances met. What was in hers he could not have said: nothing and everything, a strange flash. She dropped her eyes and he walked on.

It was no longer the simple eye of a child but a mysterious gulf half opened and abruptly closed. Hugo dwells on that first gaze of a soul that does not yet know itself, like dawn in the sky, innocent and fatal, a snare the maiden sets without knowing it, from which the flower called love springs in the depths of whoever meets it.

That evening in his garret Marius looked over his clothes and perceived for the first time that he had been going to the Luxembourg in his everyday things: a battered hat, coarse carter's boots, black trousers white at the knees and a coat pale at the elbows. He judged this slovenly, indecorous and inconceivably stupid.

title: Beginning of a Great Malady
summary: In his new coat, new hat and gloves, Marius marches on the bench like Hannibal on Rome, twice passes the girl blushing and pale, hears her voice, and retreats to sit on another bench. For the first time he thinks M. Leblanc may have noticed his assiduity, and feels the nickname irreverent. He forgets to dine and brushes his coat before bed.
details: Next day Marius put on his new coat, trousers, hat and boots, and gloves, a tremendous luxury, and set out, pretending not to see Courfeyrac on the way; Courfeyrac told his friends he had met Marius's new hat and coat with Marius inside them, looking utterly stupid, as if going to an examination. At the Luxembourg Marius circled the basin, stared at the swans and a mouldy statue, listened to a fat bourgeois instructing his small son to shun excess, and only then turned slowly toward his alley, as if both forced and forbidden to go.

Seeing M. Leblanc and the girl on their bench at the far end, he buttoned his coat to the top, smoothed it, admired the gleam of his trousers and marched on the bench as on a fortress, all the while thinking about the stupidity of the Manuel du Baccalauréat and with a whistling in his ears. His pace slackened; well short of the bench he turned back without knowing why, holding himself erect in case anyone was looking. On the next pass he got within three trees and hesitated, then with a violent effort rushed past, red to the ears, hand thrust into his coat like a statesman, not daring to look, and heard an ineffable voice that must be hers; he consoled himself that she would esteem him if she knew he was the real author of a dissertation M. François de Neufchâteau had passed off as his own. He passed again, very pale, and fancied she was gazing after him, which made him stumble.

He went no nearer, but sat down in the middle of the walk, a thing he never did, reflecting that it was hard that a white bonnet and black gown should be insensible to splendid trousers and a new coat. After a quarter of an hour he rose, stood motionless, and for the first time in fifteen months considered that the gentleman who sat there daily with his daughter had probably noticed him and found his assiduity singular; for the first time, too, he felt some irreverence in calling the stranger M. Leblanc even in thought. He traced figures in the sand with his cane, turned his back on the bench and went home. He forgot to dine, ate a bit of bread at eight, and brushed and folded his coat with great care before bed.

title: Divers Claps of Thunder Fall on Ma’am Bougon
summary: For a fortnight Marius goes daily to the Luxembourg in his new coat, to the stupefaction of the old portress, whom Courfeyrac calls Ma'am Bougon, and sits on his distant bench watching the white bonnet and the blue light without approaching.
details: Next day Ma'am Bougon, as Courfeyrac styled the old portress and principal tenant of the Gorbeau hovel (her name was really Madame Burgon), observed with stupefaction that M. Marius was going out again in his new coat. He went to the Luxembourg but no further than his bench midway along the alley, and sat there until the gates closed, making out from afar the white bonnet, the black dress and above all that blue light; he did not see M. Leblanc and his daughter leave, and weeks later could not recall where he had dined.
