On the third day Ma'am Bougon was thunderstruck, 'Three days in succession!', and tried to follow him, a hippopotamus pursuing a chamois; she lost him in two minutes and came back choking with asthma and furious. At the Luxembourg the girl was there with M. Leblanc; Marius approached as near as he dared pretending to read, retreated to his bench and spent four hours watching sparrows who seemed to mock him.

So a fortnight passed. Marius came no longer to stroll but to sit always in the same place without knowing why, putting on his new coat every morning for the purpose of not showing himself. She was decidedly a marvellous beauty; the only possible criticism was that the contrast between her melancholy gaze and her merry smile gave her face a rather wild effect, strange without ceasing to be charming.

title: Taken Prisoner
summary: M. Leblanc and his daughter walk down the alley and pass Marius's bench; she gazes at him with pensive sweetness as she goes by. Marius is set on fire, wanders the garden like a madman, treats Courfeyrac to dinner and the theatre, and babbles happily at breakfast next day. He is desperately in love.
details: Near the end of the second week Marius sat with an open book he had not turned a page of for two hours when he started: Leblanc and his daughter had risen and, arm in arm, were advancing toward the middle of the alley where he sat. He closed and opened his book and trembled; the aureole was coming straight at him and he would not have time to strike an attitude. He imagined M. Leblanc darting angry looks at him and feared the gentleman might speak to him. He dropped his head; when he raised it they were close. The girl passed and glanced at him, a steady gaze of pensive sweetness that thrilled him from head to foot, as if reproaching him for not having come to her and saying, 'I am coming myself.' He was dazzled, and at the same time horribly vexed by the dust on his boots, which he was sure she had looked at.

He followed her with his eyes until she vanished, then paced the Luxembourg like a madman, laughing and talking to himself, so dreamy near the nursemaids that each thought him in love with her. Leaving the garden in hopes of meeting her in the street, he ran into Courfeyrac under the Odéon arcades and took him to dine at Rousseau's, where he ate like an ogre, spent six francs, tipped six sous and praised a speech by Audry de Puyraveau. He treated Courfeyrac to Frédérick in L'Auberge des Adrets at the Porte-Saint-Martin and was enormously amused, yet his shyness redoubled: he refused to look at a modiste's garter and was almost horrified when Courfeyrac wished to add her to his collection.

At breakfast at the Café Voltaire next morning he ate more still, was thoughtful and merry, embraced a stranger from the provinces and, amid a discussion of Guicherat's grammars, exclaimed that it was very agreeable to have the cross. 'That's queer,' whispered Courfeyrac to Jean Prouvaire. 'No,' said Prouvaire, 'that's serious.' Marius had reached the first violent and charming hour of a grand passion; a glance had done it all. Hugo compares a woman's glance to quiet machinery past which one walks safely for years until the day it catches hold, after which one falls from gearing to gearing and emerges either disfigured by shame or transfigured by passion.

title: Adventures of the Letter U Delivered Over to Conjectures
summary: For a month Marius comes daily, hiding behind trees and statues to be seen by the girl and not by her father, while she answers his looks with hers. M. Leblanc seems to notice, moves to another bench and sometimes comes alone. Marius finds a handkerchief marked U. F. on their bench, decides her name is Ursule and worships it, though it was the old gentleman's.
details: Marius's solitude, pride, chastity and life of reverie had prepared him for passion; his worship of his father had retreated to the depths of his soul and something was needed in the foreground. Love came. For a full month he went to the Luxembourg every day; 'He is on duty,' said Courfeyrac. It was certain the girl looked at him. Grown bolder, he approached the bench but no longer passed in front of it, so as not to attract the father's attention, and posted himself behind trees and the pedestals of Leonidas or Spartacus with a book, over which his eyes sought her, while she, chatting naturally with the white-haired man, turned her profile toward him with a vague smile and bent on him the reveries of a passionate eye: her mouth answered one, her glance another.

M. Leblanc evidently noticed something. Often when Marius arrived he rose and walked about; he abandoned their usual place for the bench by the Gladiator at the other end, as if to see whether Marius would follow. Marius did not understand and followed, an error. The father grew irregular and no longer brought his daughter every day; sometimes he came alone, and then Marius did not stay, another blunder. He had passed from timidity to blindness and paid no heed.

One evening at dusk he found on the bench they had just left a plain white handkerchief, fine and seemingly perfumed, marked with the letters U. F. He knew nothing of her, neither family name, first name nor address; these two letters were the first thing of hers he possessed, and he built on them at once. U was the Christian name: 'Ursule! what a delicious name!' He kissed the handkerchief, wore it on his heart by day and slept with it at his lips by night, declaring her whole soul lay in it. The handkerchief belonged to the old gentleman, who had let it fall from his pocket. In the following days Marius showed himself at the Luxembourg only kissing it and pressing it to his heart; the beautiful child, understanding nothing, signified as much by imperceptible signs, and Marius said, 'O modesty!'

title: The Veterans Themselves Can Be Happy
summary: A gust of May wind lifts 'Ursule's' dress to the garter as she walks with M. Leblanc; Marius, who alone saw it, is furious and jealous, glares at her, and suspects a passing one-armed, wooden-legged veteran of having seen too. He sulks three days before forgiving her, and his passion grows to madness.
details: Once, Hugo admits, 'his Ursule' caused Marius serious grief. One May day she had persuaded M. Leblanc to leave the bench and stroll; father and daughter passed Marius, who stood watching them from behind. A merry gust from the nursery lifted her dress almost to the garter and a leg of exquisite shape appeared. Marius saw it, and was exasperated and furious. She hurriedly pushed her dress down with a divinely troubled gesture, but he remained angry: the alley was empty, but someone might have been there, and what she had done was horrible. The poor child had done nothing; the only culprit was the wind, but Marius, in whom the jealous Bartholo stirred within the youthful Cherubin, was determined to be vexed. The sight itself gave him no pleasure; a stranger's white stocking would have pleased him more.

When she came back past his bench he darted a sullen, ferocious glance at her; she gave the slight backward straightening and lift of the eyelids that means 'Well, what is the matter?' It was their first quarrel. At that moment a bent, wrinkled old soldier crossed the walk in a Louis XV uniform with the cross of Saint-Louis, one empty sleeve, a silver chin and a wooden leg, looking extremely well satisfied, and seemed to give Marius a fraternal, merry wink as if they had shared some good luck. Marius reached a paroxysm of jealousy: perhaps the veteran had been there, perhaps he had seen; he wanted to exterminate him.

Time blunts all points. Marius's wrath against 'Ursule', just as he thought it, passed off; he pardoned her, with great effort, after sulking for three days. And in spite of all this, and because of it, his passion grew to madness.

title: Eclipse
summary: Marius follows 'Ursule' and M. Leblanc home to a modest house in the Rue de l'Ouest and questions the porter, who asks if he is a police spy. The next evening M. Leblanc stares hard at him at the gate. The couple stop coming to the Luxembourg; Marius keeps vigil under their lit windows for a week until, one night, the windows are dark. The porter tells him the gentleman has moved away, leaving no address.
details: Knowing her name was Ursule was a great deal and very little; in three or four weeks Marius had used up that bliss and wanted to know where she lived. After the blunders of the Gladiator bench and of leaving when M. Leblanc came alone, he committed a third and immense one: he followed 'Ursule'. She lived in the Rue de l'Ouest, in its most unfrequented part, in a new, modest three-storey house, and from then on he added to the Luxembourg the happiness of following her home.

Wanting to know who she was, he one evening went in after them and asked the porter whether the gentleman who had just come in lived on the first floor. The third, said the porter; a gentleman of property, a very kind man who did good to the unfortunate though not rich himself. Asked his name, the porter raised his head: 'Are you a police spy, sir?' Marius went off abashed but delighted, having learned that Ursule was the daughter of a man of independent means living on the third floor in the Rue de l'Ouest.

Next day the couple left the Luxembourg early; Marius followed as usual, and at the carriage gate M. Leblanc let his daughter pass in, paused, and stared intently at Marius. The day after they did not come. At nightfall Marius went to the Rue de l'Ouest, saw a light on the third floor and walked beneath it until it went out. For a week he waited all day at the Luxembourg in vain and stood sentinel under the windows at night, feeding on fever; sometimes a shadow crossed the red light and his heart beat. On the eighth night there was no light; he waited until one in the morning and no one came or lit a lamp. The next evening the shades were drawn and the third floor dark. He knocked and asked the porter for the gentleman on the third floor. 'Has moved away.' Yesterday. Where to? The porter knew nothing and no address had been left. Then he looked up, recognised Marius, and said: 'So it's you! But you are decidedly a spy then?'

title: Mines and Miners
summary: Hugo describes society as undermined by layers of 'mines', religious, philosophical, economic and revolutionary, dug by disinterested thinkers from Huss down to Babeuf; far below them all lies a last mine without light, the 'third lower floor', which communicates with the abyss.
details: Every society has what the theatre calls a third lower floor: a subsoil mined in every direction, sometimes for good and sometimes for evil. The Encyclopaedia was a mine almost open to the sky; the catacombs where the first mass was said were the vaults of the world. Beneath the social structure run religious, philosophical, economic and revolutionary galleries where utopias travel, meet, fraternise and fight, and what emerges from them is the future.

The deeper one goes the more mysterious the toilers. Hugo sets them on a descending ladder, Huss, Luther, Descartes, Voltaire, Condorcet, Robespierre, Marat, Babeuf, with Saint-Simon, Owen and Fourier in side galleries, and below them dim men who perhaps do not yet exist. Different as they are, all these pioneers share one mark, disinterestedness, the starry eye that seeks the absolute; even Marat forgets himself like Jesus. The other sign is the shadowy eye, with which evil begins: fear the man who has no glance at all.

Far below all these mines, lower than Marat and Babeuf and unconnected with them, lies the last mine, the troisième dessous: the grave of shadows, the cellar of the blind, which communicates with the abyss.

title: The Lowest Depths
summary: In the lowest cavern disinterestedness vanishes and each is for himself: creatures born of ignorance and misery, driven by appetite from suffering to crime. Unlike the noble upper mine of Book IV, this cavern of theft, prostitution and murder hates everything above it; its only cure is light, since to destroy ignorance is to destroy crime.
details: In this gulf the 'I' howls and gnaws; the spectres who roam there, almost beasts, know neither the idea nor the word of progress and think only of satisfying their desires. Their two stepmothers are ignorance and misery, their guide necessity, their satisfaction appetite. Ferocious as tigers rather than tyrants, they pass from suffering to crime; hunger is the point of departure and Satan the point reached. From that vault Lacenaire emerges.

Book IV showed a compartment of the upper mine, the political and philosophical excavation, where even error is heroic and the work is called Progress. Now Hugo turns to hideous depths: the great cavern of evil beneath society, which will exist until ignorance is dissipated. It is hatred without exception, knows no philosophers, has never turned a page, and desires the destruction of everything, including the upper mines it execrates; its name is theft, prostitution, murder, and its vault is ignorance.

Everything above it aims to suppress it: destroy the cavern Ignorance and you destroy the lair Crime. The only social peril is darkness. All men are of the same clay, but ignorance mixed into that clay blackens it and turns to evil within.

title: Babet, Gueulemer, Claquesous, and Montparnasse
summary: Four ruffians ruled the underworld of Paris from 1830 to 1835: Gueulemer, a stupid colossus and cold-blooded assassin; Babet, a thin, learned ex-showman and tooth-puller who reads the papers; Claquesous, a masked ventriloquist who is only ever seen in the dark; and Montparnasse, a pretty, pomaded youth under twenty who kills to dress well.
details: Gueulemer, a Hercules of no fixed position, lairs in the sewer of the Arche-Marion: six feet tall, with marble pectorals and a bird's head, under forty but already lined, a great idle force whose muscles want work and whose stupidity refuses it. He is an assassin through coolness, thought to be a creole, possibly mixed up in the death of Marshal Brune while a porter at Avignon in 1815.

Babet is Gueulemer's contrast: thin, learned, transparent but impenetrable, a talker who underlines his smiles. He has acted in vaudeville, sold plaster busts of the head of State, pulled teeth in a fairground booth under a grandiloquent poster, had and lost a wife and children as one loses a handkerchief, and, rare in his world, reads the newspapers; he once regretted that his wife had not given him a child with a calf's muzzle, which would have made a fortune. Later he gave up everything to 'undertake Paris'.

Claquesous is night. He appears only after dark and returns to a hole no one knows before dawn, speaks to his accomplices with his back turned in total darkness, puts on a mask if a candle is brought, and is a ventriloquist; Babet calls him a nocturne for two voices. No one is sure he has a name, a voice or a face. Montparnasse is a child under twenty with a handsome face, cherry lips and spring in his eyes, who has every vice and aspires to every crime: a street boy turned pickpocket turned garrotter, genteel, effeminate, ferocious, with a curled hat-brim, a threadbare coat of the best cut, a flower in his buttonhole and a bludgeon in his pocket. The first grisette who called him handsome made a Cain of this Abel; wanting elegance, hence idleness, hence crime, he had numerous corpses behind him at eighteen. A dandy of the sepulchre.

title: Composition of the Troupe
summary: The four ruffians form one many-headed robber called Patron-Minette, who contract for the ambushes of the Seine department and hire out accomplices for crimes planned by others, meeting at nightfall on the waste ground by the Salpêtrière. Hugo lists their troupe, including Brujon and the road-mender Boulatruelle, and ends by calling for light to be cast on society from below.
details: The four were a Proteus, slipping among the police under different names, lending each other aliases and hiding-places, now shrinking to a single man, now multiplying into a throng: not four men but one mysterious robber with four heads, the monstrous polyp of evil in the crypt of society. Through their network they held the general enterprise of ambushes in the Seine department; men of nocturnal imagination brought them ideas, and they supplied the scenery and the troupe, underletting their accomplices to any crime that needed muscle and paid well. They met at nightfall, the hour they woke, on the plains beside the Salpêtrière and planned their twelve black hours.

The underworld called the association Patron-Minette, an old popular term for daybreak, probably from the hour at which their work ended and phantoms vanish. When the presiding judge asked Lacenaire who had committed a crime he denied, he answered, 'Perhaps it was Patron-Minette.' Hugo gives the troupe's roll of names: Panchaud alias Printanier alias Bigrenaille, Brujon (of a whole dynasty of Brujons), Boulatruelle the road-mender already met, Laveuve, Finistère, Homère-Hogu, Mardisoir, Dépêche, Fauntleroy alias the Flower Girl, Glorieux a discharged convict, Barrecarrosse called Monsieur Dupont, L'Esplanade-du-Sud, Poussagrive, Carmagnolet, Kruideniers called Bizarro, Mangedentelle, Les-pieds-en-l'Air, Demi-Liard called Deux-Milliards, and others; each name is a species of fungus from the underside of civilisation.

These men were not seen by day; worn out by their nights they slept in limekilns, abandoned quarries at Montmartre or Montrouge, or sewers. They still exist, Hugo says, and always have; individuals are extirpated but the tribe subsists, reborn from the social ooze under new names. They scent purses and watches, patiently stalk bourgeois with a 'stealable' air, and, met at midnight on a deserted boulevard, seem not men but forms of living mist detached from the night. What makes such spectres vanish? Light, in floods; no bat resists the dawn. Light up society from below.
